title: What low-level design is
idea: Low-level design (LLD) decides the classes, their responsibilities, the methods they expose and how they collaborate, so that one feature's code stays correct and easy to change.

analogy.text: An architect's floor plan shows rooms and doors. The joiner's drawing shows each cupboard: its parts, hinges and which wall it hangs on.
analogy.breaks: Cupboards rarely change after fitting; classes change every sprint.

points: LLD names the types: entities, value objects, interfaces and the services using them.
Each class gets one job, owns its data and guards its own rules.
Variation hides behind an interface, so a new option means a new class.
Good LLD shows when requirements change: edits land in one place, not five.

steps.caption: Start from the requirement, not from code. It names the nouns: parcel, shipping option, fee.
`Parcel` is a value object. Its constructor rejects a weight of zero or less, so bad data never travels.
`ShippingMethod` is the contract. Fee and delivery days live together, so neither can be forgotten.
`FlatPlusWeight` covers every base-plus-per-kilogram tariff with data, not new if-branches.
Same-day delivery arrives later. It becomes `SameDay`, a new class; no existing class is edited.
The caller only knows the interface. That one decision is what keeps the feature cheap to change.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: Working code with no design: string keys, rules scattered across methods, bad input accepted silently.

walk.text: Every tariff sits in one method chosen by a string. Each new option edits it.
An unknown key falls through to zero. A typo means free shipping, with no error.
Lower-case `express` and a negative weight both run. Nothing owns the rule that weight is positive.
Delivery days repeat the same keys elsewhere. Someone added same-day to fees and forgot it here.
So same-day prints four days. The compiler cannot help, because the link is only a string.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: The same feature after LLD: a value object, a contract, and one class per kind of tariff.

walk.text: `Parcel` checks its own invariant in the compact constructor. An invalid parcel cannot exist.
`ShippingMethod` bundles fee and days, so adding an option means writing both.
`FlatPlusWeight` is a record: immutable, validated, and reused for every tariff of that shape.
`SameDay` is the new requirement. It is added beside the others, not wedged into them.
The caller loops over the interface. It never asks which concrete class it holds.
The bad weight now fails loudly at the boundary, with a message naming the value.

pitfalls: Choosing behaviour with string or int codes; a typo compiles and silently takes the default branch.
Repeating the same if-else chain in several methods; one gets missed when an option is added.
Leaving validation to callers; one forgetful caller lets invalid objects spread through the system.

quiz.q: A new rule: Express is free above 20 kg. In the fixed design, what changes?
options: The Parcel record gets a free flag
A new ShippingMethod class for Express's tariff
The ShippingMethod interface gains a method
quiz.why: Editing `FlatPlusWeight` would also change Standard. A new `ShippingMethod` class holds the 20 kg rule; callers, `Parcel` and `FlatPlusWeight` stay unchanged.

takeaway: LLD gives each rule one home, so change touches one class.

starters: How is LLD different from just writing clean code?
When is an interface overkill for a small feature?
Why use a record for Parcel instead of a normal class?
